**(B)** Orchid

Orchids grow as epiphytes on the branches of huge trees in dense rain forests, where the air is moist and the light is shaded; their velamen roots absorb moisture from the humid air. *Opuntia* is a xerophyte adapted to deserts, mangroves are halophytes of saline swamps, and the lotus is an aquatic plant (hydrophyte).

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives that orchids, as rain-forest epiphytes, thrive in moist, shady conditions.]

**(C)** Superposed phyllotaxy

In opposite superposed phyllotaxy, each node bears a pair of leaves and each next pair stands directly above the one below, so all pairs lie in one plane (e.g. Jamun). In decussate phyllotaxy the next pair is at right angles, so the pairs lie in two planes (e.g. *Calotropis*). Alternate phyllotaxy has a single leaf per node and whorled has many leaves per node.

**(C)** epigynous

When the thalamus encloses the ovary, the ovary lies below the other three whorls (inferior ovary) and the flower is epigynous, e.g. sunflower and guava. The style carries the stigma up above the other whorls, so a tall stigma does not change this. In a hypogynous flower the ovary is the highest part, and in a perigynous flower the ovary and other whorls are at about the same level, which is the half-superior, half-inferior condition.

**(B)** Beet is a root but Arum is a stem

Beet (*Beta vulgaris*) is a napiform tap root swollen with stored food. *Arum* stores food in a corm, a swollen underground stem, like its relative *Colocasia*. So they are two different types: a modified root and a modified stem.

[Note: the chapter does not name *Arum*; standard biology gives that *Arum* perennates by a corm, an underground stem.]
